items.title: Ernest "Punch" Miller Interview, 1959-08-20
items.q: There was one fella that I really wish would have did something like a record or some kind of something before he died. I liked him so much, that was Buddy Petit.

ctx.x: Yeah, Dave Bailey. Yeah, well that's Ernest Johnson's brother. See? They must be half brother. But anyhow, they were always there, we were out in front of town there on Chippy Ward in St. Thomas. That's where they lived then. And what made me go out there, it was a boy out in the army, what he did now, I forget his name, but his mother lived out there and he told me to come and I could stay with him. That's how we were good friends in the army see? So he brought me there and they really treated me nice. I lived…
Well nobody's found it yet. I've heard talk of his record. He's supposed to have made, but you never know.

items.title: Ernest "Punch" Miller Interview, 1957-multiple
items.q: Buddy Petit was one of the fellas... Buddy Petit was my idea all the time. I liked him all the time.

ctx.x: You remember some of the other good musicians around here? You said you played in Jack Carey's band. Who were some of the other bands, the other trumpet players you heard when you first came here?

When I first came here? Yeah. Well, Buddy Petit was one of the fellas, Ray and Plinistain. And Kid René. And Louis too, Louis Armstrong. He was cracking them up. But the idea about Louis, he always played off like the Capitol Boat. And going off something, you know, like that. He'd play in brass bands every now and then, but he wasn't exactly with us, because he always looked like a little above that, or some kind of really. Yeah. Big time people would hire him all the time, you know. He'd work with a kid, Ori,…
Louis thought you meant it though, huh, did he? Yeah. Louis thought they were going to hire you in this place?

items.title: Ernest "Punch" Miller Interview, 1957-multiple
items.q: Buddy 15 and me and Louie and Chris Kelly and Sam Morgan all of them in front of them.

ctx.x: Sure. Sure, I know him. Where was he from? Do you remember anybody? Tell him he's from Milwaukee. I don't know. I don't know. Guys, that guy didn't tell you where the real home was. But we had a fella named Ed Ellis used to play trombone. Talked properly, you know. Every time somebody asked him, he was a little bit of a guitar.

I was wondering about somebody at that. Did you know Jimmy Blank, the piano player? Sure. I know him. I know him. I know him. I know him. I know him. I know him. I know him. I know him. I know him. I know him. I know him. But stuff says New York. So I asked him again, he says, tell him my home is in Philly. So he got sick, see. And he got really sick. Didn't nobody know what to do for everybody. So where was his people and everything. So he called his wife. His wife was named Stella. He said, what is it? He said,…
I believe he left there in 22 didn't he? Joe, I think before then, 1918. Yeah, I didn't know him. He was in the Army when he left here again. Sure, I didn't know him.

items.title: Ernest 'Punch' Miller Interview, 1959-09-25
items.q: Buddy Petit had a style, just was hard to get into... He could play a real good horn.

ctx.x: I see. Well who did Buddy Petit play like? Anybody today or any other record jammer?

Well I've been trying to figure that out. Buddy Petit had a style, just was hard to get into, you know. I can blow a lot like him, but I just can't keep his style up going, cause he could go way down and get them pedal notes, you know, bring one of them, diminished chords and things and all like that. He could play a real good horn.
Was Joe Oliver doing anything like him at all?
